repos.title: SubRoformer: Subband Time-Domain Representation for Music Source Separation
repos.paper_summary: SubRoFormer is a Transformer-based music source separation system that splits a stereo mix into frequency-localized subbands, runs a separator on temporally compressed features, and predicts complex masks at 100 Hz. The subband module uses an overlapping triangular FIR filter bank, complex analytic conversion, baseband demodulation, and decimation, with a fast polyphase implementation. The separator combines a patched axial RoFormer (alternating subband-axis and temporal-axis attention with rotary embeddings) with a GEGLU gated residual fusion that merges coarse and fine-rate features. On MUSDB18-HQ, training only on that dataset, the target-specific models reach an average SDR of 10.63 dB across four stems, 0.61 dB above the strongest complete public-data BS-RoFormer result the authors report, and 0.99 dB above the reported Mel-RoFormer result. BS-RoFormer is 1.38 dB better on bass. With 500 extra training songs, a single multi-stem model reaches 11.59 dB. The subband transform alone reconstructs the mixture at 27.8 dB SDR-scale fidelity for mel and ERB banks, far below the near-perfect STFT and MDCT controls. The authors state the results are single-seed and directional, and that repeated seeds, efficiency measurements, and parameter-matched ablations are still needed.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Subband frontend plus a residual RoFormer separator targets the time-frequency trade-off in music source separation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior systems span waveform, hybrid, spectrogram, and subband separators, and the paper positions itself among them.

digest_headlines.heading: Subband Time-Domain Representation
digest_headlines.headline: A fixed triangular subband filter bank with polyphase implementation reconstructs the mixture with measured distortion.

digest_headlines.heading: Residual SubRoFormer
digest_headlines.headline: SubRoFormer combines fine-rate features, a patched axial RoFormer, and gated residual fusion to predict complex masks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use MUSDB18-HQ with SDR as the primary metric, and training data and augmentation are described.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: SubRoFormer-B reaches 10.63 dB on MUSDB18-HQ without extra data, but the authors call the evidence preliminary.

repos.title: Reinforcing End-to-End Autonomous Driving Safety via Negative-Aware Planning in a Unified World-Action Model
repos.paper_summary:
NegWAM is a safety post-training method for unified world-action models (WAMs), which jointly predict future video and driving actions. It starts from a pretrained WAM and adds a second training stage that uses offline-mined failure trajectories. Negatives come from the 16K-trajectory GTRS vocabulary: candidates within 1.0 m ADE of the expert that score zero EPDMS on the NAVSIM v2 metric cache. During training, up to 16 negatives per scene serve as repulsive anchors in a distance-adaptive hinge loss and as clean rider tokens that a contrastive ranking loss scores against the expert. The flow-matching loss stays active, and the riders and scoring head are discarded at inference.

On NAVSIM v2, NegWAM reaches 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1% relative gain over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and 93.3 EPDMS on navtest. The paper also reports zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM.

Limitations: mining requires an offline EPDMS evaluator and per-scene metric caches, so negative selection depends on privileged evaluation. Only 85.8% of training samples yield at least one valid negative, and the median negative ADE is 0.80 m, with about 9% falling within 0.3 to 0.5 m.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: World-action models learn only from expert trajectories, leaving nearby unsafe alternatives unconstrained, which motivates safety post-training.

digest_headlines.heading: Literature Review
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work shows near-expert failures are useful supervision, but unified world-action models do not explicitly contrast expert trajectories with them.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Near-expert failures mined offline supply repulsive anchor and scene-compatibility losses added to flow-matching post-training.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments and Results
digest_headlines.headline: NegWAM reaches 40.4 EPDMS on navhard and 93.3 on navtest, a 4.1 % relative gain over the strongest scorer-free baseline.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: NegWAM adds no inference overhead, but its generalization to diverse real-world driving remains to be established.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers training configuration, full navtest component scores, additional qualitative cases, failure cases, and limits of the negative supervision.

repos.title: PersonaAgent: Retrieval-Augmented Transaction Anomaly Scoring with Refreshable Multi-Entity Persona Memory
repos.paper_summary: PersonaAgent is a transaction anomaly detection framework that stores entity behavior in a refreshable Semantic Persona Memory and feeds it into frozen production detectors through lightweight adapters. LLM agents design the persona protocol offline, using a development set and a prespecified selection rule. A weekly batch job recomputes five numerical persona views, covering card spending, Merchant, MCC, and Location topics, and MCC-topic–Location-topic interactions, with no LLM calls. Each adapter combines retrieved records, activity shares, and the frozen base score through tree-based encoders and a small neural network. At Visa, across four detectors, the method lifts PR-AUC by 0.65–6.58% and the business metric BM1 by 8.93–14.24%, both relative, in deployment. A 1,000-transaction CPU batch is scored in 1–2 ms. Three of four group views outperform matched conventional clustering in standalone prediction. Limitations: BM1 gains shrink when topic and interaction records are one week old, location-derived signals may correlate with sensitive attributes, and the evaluation uses proprietary data from one company.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Entity behavior changes faster than detector releases, so the paper stores behavior in refreshable persona memory outside frozen detectors.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans transaction models, retrieval-augmented scoring, and agentic optimization, and PersonaAgent differs by keeping language models offline.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries and Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Adapters must use only evidence available by each memory cutoff, while detectors stay frozen and metrics are relative to the base.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A design-time agent search builds a persona protocol, a weekly batch refreshes memory, and per-detector adapters score transactions deterministically.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: PersonaAgent improved all four frozen detectors on every metric in both the held-out test and live deployment.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Stable topic identities and versioned packages let entity knowledge update without detector releases, though gains shrink with older records.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: One validated release package improved four detectors offline and in deployment, with business metric gains of 8.93–14.24% relative.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists privacy and compliance terms, deployment controls, persona record fields, fallback rules, search algorithms, and supplementary diagnostics.

repos.title: TerraMesh-Masks: Open-Vocabulary Segmentation for Earth Observation
repos.paper_summary:
TerraMesh-Masks is a dataset of 16 million binary segmentation masks, each paired with a multimodal TerraMesh Earth observation sample at 10 m resolution. It also includes TerraMesh-Masks-Eval, an expert-reviewed benchmark of 523 masks covering over 200 classes. Masks are built from OpenStreetMap and Overture Maps geometries, filtered by area and NDVI-based sampling, and scored by Mistral-Large-3, with masks above 0.5 kept. The authors adapt TerraMind into TerraMind-OVS, which predicts 196 mask tokens conditioned on a CLIP text embedding of the class query, and continue pretraining it on the dataset.

On the evaluation set, the best model, TerraMind-OVS-L with S2 input, reaches 35.18% IoUpos. The comparison points are 16.29% for DINOv3.txt, 11.33% for SAM-3, and 21.59% for SegEarth-OV, the strongest EO-specific baseline. Each IoUpos result has a 95% confidence interval of about ±3.4 points, so differences between closely matched checkpoints are not reliable.

Limitations: the vocabulary covers only static land cover and infrastructure, so clouds, floods, and snow are not segmented. Labels are generated automatically and contain noise. Coverage follows OpenStreetMap, which is denser in Europe and North America, and only 13 of the 523 evaluation samples lie above 60° latitude.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Open-vocabulary segmentation lacks large satellite datasets and benchmarks, which the paper addresses with TerraMesh-Masks and an evaluation set.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing remote-sensing open-vocabulary datasets mostly use high-resolution imagery and cover few semantic classes.

digest_headlines.heading: TerraMesh-Masks
digest_headlines.headline: TerraMesh-Masks adds roughly 16 million language-labelled masks to nine million TerraMesh patches, built from OpenStreetMap and Overture Maps.

digest_headlines.heading: TerraMind-OVS
digest_headlines.headline: TerraMind-OVS treats binary masks as an extra modality, predicting mask tokens conditioned on a text query.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental setup
digest_headlines.headline: TerraMind small, base, and large are continually pretrained on TerraMesh-Masks for 15B tokens, 3% of original training.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: TerraMind-OVS reaches 35.18% IoU against 16.29% for DINOv3.txt, the strongest generalist baseline.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limits are a static vocabulary, noisy automatic labels, bias toward Europe and North America, and a small evaluation set.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that the dataset and baselines could support scalable, modality-aware open-vocabulary segmentation in Earth observation.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The work is funded by a European Space Agency lab through a named project under a contract.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists TerraMesh details, dataset statistics, large language model prompts, filtering, training, and extra analyses.

repos.title: Doubly-robust causal inference for multi-valued treatment regimes with recurrent neural networks
repos.paper_summary:
This paper extends longitudinal targeted minimum loss-based estimation (LTMLE) to multi-valued treatments by fitting one multinomial treatment model per time point rather than several binary regressions. It uses recurrent neural networks (RNNs) as learners for the outcome, treatment, and censoring models. The target is the expected outcome under static, dynamic, and stochastic treatment rules, identified via the g-formula under sequential unconfoundedness, consistency, and positivity.

In simulations comparing LTMLE and sequential g-computation, each with ensemble machine learning (SL) or RNNs, plus inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), LTMLE with SL or RNNs is approximately unbiased with close to nominal coverage. Sequential g-computation with SL is biased by up to 0.059 under the dynamic rule. Multinomial and binomial treatment models perform similarly with SL, but the multinomial model gives more stable inference with RNN treatment models.

The paper reports under-coverage: LTMLE-RNN covers below nominal at t=36 under the stochastic rule, and LTMLE coverage is lower at later times under the dynamic rule. The authors attribute the RNN under-coverage to optimistic influence-curve variance estimates from networks fit without cross-fitting. Positivity violations remain a concern.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing targeted estimators handle only binary or continuous treatments, so the paper extends LTMLE to multi-valued treatments with recurrent neural networks.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivating example: safety effects of antipsychotic treatment regimes
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier antipsychotic comparisons found lower diabetes risk with haloperidol, olanzapine, and risperidone than with aripiprazole.

digest_headlines.heading: Doubly-robust estimation
digest_headlines.headline: Estimation combines sequential g-computation, inverse probability weighting, and LTMLE, with RNN learners for each nuisance model.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulations
digest_headlines.headline: At month 36, many rule-followers have low cumulative treatment probability under static and dynamic rules, less so with RNNs.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: A multinomial treatment model gives more stable inference than binomial models when treatment models are RNNs.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: LTMLE is approximately unbiased in these simulations, and positivity violations and separate propensity fitting remain open problems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the data-generating equations, a causal graph figure, and the treatment-effect definitions.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Supporting tables give hyperparameters, metric definitions, performance and positivity results, and computation times for each estimator.

repos.title: When Imperfect Automated Fact-Checking Backfires: Social Learning in the Presence of Misinformation
repos.paper_summary: This paper studies when a free, error-prone automated fact-checking tool can lower welfare in a sequential social learning model of misinformation. Agents arrive in order, observe each article's reliability and their predecessors' like or dislike actions, and may pay a cost K to fact-check. Manual checking is perfectly accurate. The automated tool has type-I and type-II error rates e1 and e2, with e1 + e2 < 1. Welfare is the probability of a correct cascade. The tool has two opposing effects: broader checking helps agents escape wrong cascades, but its errors can mislead agents who would otherwise verify the article correctly. The authors prove that adding the tool strictly lowers welfare for articles of intermediate reliability when truthful articles are not too informative and manual checking is sufficiently costly. Simulations show the tool can help on either side of that intermediate range, and that it improves on manual-only checking on average only above a threshold accuracy. The model assumes verdicts are independent given veracity; correlated or identical verdicts are left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Free, error-prone fact-checking tools can mislead others through actions, so their effect on collective learning depends on conditions.

digest_headlines.heading: The Model
digest_headlines.headline: Agents with heterogeneous priors observe article reliability and predecessors' actions, and may pay to fact-check before liking or disliking.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem of Welfare Change
digest_headlines.headline: Welfare change decomposes into reliability-weighted changes for truthful and fake articles under symmetric assumptions.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulations and Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: A proof certifies welfare loss for intermediate reliability when truthful articles are weakly informative, and simulations show gains elsewhere.

digest_headlines.heading: CONCLUSIONS
digest_headlines.headline: Automated tools raise average welfare only above a threshold accuracy, so platforms should not offer them before that point.

digest_headlines.heading: APPENDIX
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives belief and checking-value derivations, cutoffs, and proofs of the cascade theorem and its lemmas.

repos.title: GTAFL: Addressing Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning in Medical Image
repos.paper_summary:
GTAFL is a federated learning framework for long-tailed image classification when the test-time class distribution is unknown. It trains three expert classifiers, targeting forward, uniform, and backward long-tail priors, on a shared feature extractor. Clients sample data with GI-GDS, which uses local inverse-frequency weights when the local and global class distributions diverge (cosine similarity below 0.9). The server retrains each expert on global federated features, synthetic features optimized to match aggregated class-wise gradients, then refines the extractor with SimCLR on unlabeled images. At inference, the three experts make an equally weighted vote.

On CIFAR10-LT, GTAFL averages 75.02% accuracy over 11 test distributions, compared with 73.69% for CReFF and 42.13% for FedGraB. The averages are 77.71% on PathMNIST-LT (CReFF 76.13%) and 66.42% on OCTMNIST-LT (BalanceFL 53.76%). The authors state that accuracy on majority classes under backward distributions is relatively modest, and that very large λ values degrade gradient matching for the federated features. Experiments cover CIFAR10-LT and two medical datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Federated learning on long-tailed medical data assumes uniform test sets, so GTAFL targets unknown test distributions.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries and Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Formal setup defines federated learning, the imbalance factor, and the objective over forward, uniform, and backward test distributions.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation and Overview
digest_headlines.headline: Each distribution-specific classifier performs best on its own test distribution, which motivates retraining one expert per distribution.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Method has four components: sampling weights interpolating local and global signals, expert classifier retraining on synthetic features, self-supervised refinement, and weighted voting.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use three datasets with imbalance factor 50, 20 clients, and six baseline federated methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: GTAFL reaches 75.02% average accuracy on CIFAR10-LT, above CReFF's 73.69%, and the best average on both medical datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work groups long-tailed and test-agnostic methods, and the authors claim to be first to formulate this federated task.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Privacy risks from gradient inversion are discussed, with differential privacy proposed as compatible but unevaluated, and majority-class accuracy noted as a limitation.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that GTAFL outperforms long-tailed federated baselines across three datasets and distribution shifts.

repos.title: A Unified Fractal Impedance Control Framework
repos.paper_summary: This paper presents H-PMP, a controller that nests a task-space admittance or HapFIC controller inside a joint-space HapFIC. It also presents the FIC Suite, an open-source toolkit with ROS2, MuJoCo, and hardware drivers for Fractal Impedance Controllers (FIC). The task layer maps the desired pose and external wrench to joint torques through the Jacobian transpose. The joint layer applies the FIC effort function, whose saturations bound the admittance offset so the controller moves between admittance and impedance behaviour. The Suite offers a desktop and web GUI, live tuning of effort profiles, and a 1 kHz robot node. A new robot needs a driver and a YAML file. On a Kinova Gen3, three experiments (trajectory tracking, a wall press with sudden loss of contact, and learning-by-demonstration) compare H-PMP with earlier FIC architectures. The excerpt reports no tracking-error, force, or timing values from these runs, so the claim of no computational overhead has no measured support there. The conclusion's efficiency argument compares the MCU's rated maximum power (about 400 mW) with a 15 to 17 W board, not a measured run. Online adaptive tuning is stated as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Robots in unstructured settings need interaction control that trades admittance against impedance, and this paper packages FIC into one library.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Redundant robots were restricted to one mode, and earlier trade-off methods risked instability, which FIC addresses through passivity.

digest_headlines.heading: The FIC Suite
digest_headlines.headline: One FIC Studio graphical interface drives MuJoCo simulation and vendor hardware through the same library and profile files, tested so far on two arms.

digest_headlines.heading: FIC Controllers
digest_headlines.headline: H-PMP nests a task-space admittance controller inside a joint-space FIC layer, with a shared FIC effort function underneath.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Validation
digest_headlines.headline: Three experiments on a Kinova Gen3 arm compare H-PMP with three other FIC architectures on tracking, contact loss and demonstration.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: H-PMP balances impedance and admittance, and the authors name adaptive online tuning as the next step.

repos.title: TCSExam: Evaluating Frontier LLMs on the Full Range of TCS Research
repos.paper_summary: TCSExam is a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents across four theoretical computer science research tracks: theorem proving in Lean 4, solver engineering, explicit constructions, and open-conjecture prove-or-refute tasks. TCSExam-Full has 100 expert-reviewed tasks, and TCSExam-Lite has 20 tasks, five per track. Every submission is checked by the Lean kernel or an executable checker. Theorem and solver scores use per-attempt success and a Kimi K3-relative metric, and an aggregate TCSExam Index combines the tracks. On Full, GPT-6 Astra leads with an Index of 71.9 and a 70.0% complete-proof rate on 20 theorems without supplied lemmas. On Lite, Opus 5.5 leads with 72.3. Full and Lite rankings agree at Spearman ρ=0.93 across eight shared agents. Open-conjecture resolution is near zero for all agents, with the highest at 5.6% for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on Full. The paper reports that solver submissions improved some public references and that one construction exceeded its task reference. Limitations: each track has only five to 30 tasks, and Lite uses a single attempt per task for most agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks cover parts of theoretical computer science, so TCSExam adds proofs, solvers, constructions, and open conjectures.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks cover proofs, solvers, or conjectures separately, and only TCSExam covers all four.

digest_headlines.heading: TCSExam
digest_headlines.headline: TCSExam assigns each task to one of four tracks, each with its own required output and success criterion.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Eight agents run on Full and nine on Lite, each attempt limited to a 12-hour development budget.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: GPT-6 Astra leads Full with an Index of 71.9, and Opus 5.5 leads Lite with 72.3.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The framework covers four research tracks, and Lite retains them while reducing attempts by 80%.

digest_headlines.heading: AI Use Statement
digest_headlines.headline: AI assistants helped author tasks, build checkers, and draft text, and the authors take responsibility for the content.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendices list the task catalogue, agent configurations, proof and solver details, and per-attempt results.

repos.title: AttnSR: Attention Step Reward for Long-Horizon Agentic RL
repos.paper_summary:
AttnSR is a step-level reward augmentation method for PPO in long-horizon LLM agent training. It derives intermediate rewards from the policy model's own attention, extracted during actor replay for old log-probabilities, so it needs no separately trained reward model and no additional rollouts. Attention is traced backward from the terminal step through a step dependency graph, with recency correction, layer fusion, and a confidence gate. The outcome reward, relative to a running baseline, sets the sign and scale of the intermediate rewards.

In a controlled study with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and LoRA training, ALFWorld success rises from 91.2% to 97.1% against terminal-only PPO on 274 held-out tasks. A positional-shaping ablation reaches 92.3%. On ScienceWorld, the method reports higher official scores at all four checkpoints and 29.9% fewer mean environment steps. WebShop shows no statistically detectable gain. Significance uses an exact McNemar test and a paired bootstrap, with one training run per method.

Limitations: attention is treated as a heuristic relevance signal, not evidence of causal contribution, and the shaped return is not guaranteed to preserve the optimal policy. Wall-clock and memory overheads are unmeasured, and the evaluated trajectories are fairly short.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Outcome-only RL gives little per-step supervision to long-horizon LLM agents, so AttnSR derives step rewards from policy attention.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Terminal-only PPO puts the outcome at the final step, and AttnSR adds signed intermediate rewards without changing that final reward.

digest_headlines.heading: AttnSR: Actor Attention for Step Credit
digest_headlines.headline: Attention is traced backward from the final step, gated by confidence, and centered on outcome to set signed step rewards.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Paired tests show the ALFWorld gain at p=0.002, while the ScienceWorld gain does not survive multiple-comparison correction.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Other agent credit methods use rollouts, learned evaluators or value estimation changes, whereas AttnSR changes only the reward interface.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: AttnSR raises ALFWorld success from 91.2% to 97.1% under PPO, with no detectable WebShop gain and one run per method.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists checkpoint scores, ALFWorld family results, hyperparameters, paired significance, trajectory diagnostics and notation.
